summary:
Ciudad Autónoma de Melilla stands under the national framework of Spain. Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative route that replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules.

Melilla has no autonomous LGTBI or gender-identity statute. An index of Spain's regional LGTBI legislation states expressly that Ceuta and Melilla have no autonomous LGTBI laws and rely on the national framework and central-government equality policies. National criminal law and national equality law govern in the city, and the national police force polices it.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months; both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence. Ley 4/2023 did reform the offences against sexual freedom at Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Courts are applying the aggravation in practice. In Vigo, a Tribunal de Instancia used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300. In Valencia, a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, while two minors were judged separately.

Hate speech on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity has been banned since 1995, with crime-law penalty enhancements for such motives. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied nationwide since July 2005.
tangentialFactors:
Melilla shares its framework-only position with Ceuta: both autonomous cities lack a regional LGTBI statute, so the pattern across Spain is that the 17 mainland autonomous communities have legislated while the two autonomous cities have not.

Ley 4/2023 was approved in the Cortes Generales on 16 February 2023 by a vote of 191 to 60, with 91 abstentions, indicating a contested but passed national measure rather than a settled consensus.

Spain is recognised in comparative rankings as among the most LGBT-friendly countries, a general national assessment that does not disaggregate conditions in Melilla.
localsOnly:
A registry for unmarried same-sex couples was created in the autonomous city of Melilla in 2008, alongside Ceuta in 1998 and all 17 mainland communities, granting unmarried couples benefits regarded as mainly symbolic. This registry is not an LGTBI or gender-identity statute.

Ley 4/2023 also regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16, and recognition of gender identity is possible from age 12 under conditions, provisions that govern residents rather than short-term visitors.

Rectification of the gender mention is an administrative procedure conducted directly before the Civil Registry, so residents can complete the change without judicial involvement or medical certification.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied to residents nationwide since July 2005.
outOfScopeNotes:
No per-city hate-offence figures, incident counts or enforcement data for Melilla were retrievable from this inventory. The absence of such counts is unresolved and should not be read as evidence that gender-motivated offences do not occur or are not recorded.

Entry, visa and border-document screening rules applicable to trans travellers arriving in Melilla are not sourced here; the inventory addresses domestic law only, and no finding on port-of-entry treatment can be made from it.

Whether the national police in Melilla operate dedicated channels for reporting gender-motivated incidents, and how such complaints are processed locally, is not sourced and remains unresolved.

The comparative ranking placing Spain among the most LGBT-friendly countries is cited without its methodology, date of assessment or sub-national breakdown.
